title: The lifespan of the Tathagata (Kern ch. 15)
hookLine: the Buddha reveals he awakened countless ages ago and is always present

lines: A PRINCE, A TREE, NEAR GAYA.
cards: A prince of the Sakya clan leaves his palace, sits under a tree near the town of Gaya, and wakes up. Not so long ago. That's what makes yesterday's crowd from under the earth impossible.
Before he explains, the Buddha does something unusual. More than once he says: trust what I'm about to tell you. And more than once, the whole assembly asks him to go on.
A teacher who asks for trust before speaking is about to say something hard to hear.

teach.b: First, the story the world believes. Gods and people all think, the Buddha says, that Shakyamuni left the Sakya palace and woke at the seat near Gaya.
Second, what he actually says: it's been ages beyond reckoning since I awoke. He reaches for a picture like chapter seven's, only larger.

Grind whole worlds into dust and drop a grain each time you pass a vast stretch of worlds, until the dust runs out. Then grind every world you passed, landed on or not, into dust, and let each grain be an age.
More time than that has gone by since he woke, and all through it he has been here in this world, teaching.
Third, why he seems to leave. If people could see him every day, the ones with little root of goodness would grow lazy, take him for granted, and stop feeling that meeting a Buddha is rare.
So he appears to pass into nirvana. He calls it a skillful means, and tomorrow he tells a story about a doctor to explain it. Fourth, the verses.

He is always here, he says, on the mountain called Vulture Peak, teaching. People with confused eyes don't see him, even when he's near. When people long to see him with their whole heart, he and his assembly appear.
Some schools treat this chapter as the heart of the whole sutra. Its claim is simple and enormous: the Buddha hasn't left.
In its words, he is always here, and people just don't always see him.

how: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, this chapter is often recited, especially its verses, and some schools, including Tiantai and Nichiren traditions, treat it as the heart of the sutra.

games.q: what does “the lifespan of the tathagata” mean?
o: the length of time a monk must train before teaching
the number of years the Buddha lived as a prince
the Buddha's life beyond measure: awake for ages, always here

p: where the world thinks he first woke
fewer than the ages since he woke
where the verses say he always is

s: the chapter says the Buddha first woke up under the tree near Gaya
that's what the world believes, he says. he woke ages beyond reckoning ago.
the Buddha calls his passing away a skillful means
he appears to leave so people won't grow lazy or take him for granted.
seeing the Buddha every day would make people more devoted, the chapter says
it says the opposite: some would grow lazy and stop feeling a Buddha is rare.

games.q: you're the Buddha. you could stay visible forever, but people who see you every day start taking you for granted. what do you do?
o: stay visible: people will figure it out.
appear to pass away, so they'll value the teaching.
games.why: he appears to pass into nirvana, though he's always here. the chapter calls it a skillful means, and tomorrow's story explains it.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is far from you, in another city, another country, or, if it feels right, someone no longer living. Notice what of them you still carry, a phrase they use, the way they laugh, a thing they taught you.
Rest with them nearby for a few breaths, as close as the breath.

wordCard.voice: The lifespan of the Tathagata. Awake for ages beyond counting, teaching all along, seeming to pass away only so people won't take him for granted. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: the Buddha's name for himself, often explained as the one thus gone, or thus come.

carryVoice: Your line: always here. Not always seen, he says, but here all along. See you tomorrow.
